question: What made you want to study Operations Management specifically, rather than a broader business degree?
lookingFor: Genuine motivation grounded in a real experience of seeing how things get made or delivered, not a generic love of business.

bullets: Name a specific moment or experience that revealed the process side of a business, not just its products
Explain what specifically excites you about operations rather than marketing, finance, or general management
Show this is a considered choice, not a fallback because you couldn't decide
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I worked weekend shifts at a small bakery, and I kept noticing how one badly timed oven run could throw off the whole morning, from what was on the shelf to how long the queue got. That got me reading about how bigger operations solve exactly that problem, and I realised what actually excites me isn't the product itself but the system that reliably produces it. Marketing and finance never grabbed me the same way, because they're about persuading or measuring, while operations is about actually making something work smoothly and repeatably.

commonMistakes: Saying 'I like business' with nothing operations-specific
Confusing operations with just logistics or delivery vans
Offering no personal anecdote or experience to ground the choice
followUps: How is operations management different from supply chain management, in your view?

question: Why do you want to study Operations Management at our university specifically?
lookingFor: Specific, researched reasons tied to the actual course, not generic praise that could apply anywhere.

bullets: Name a specific module, professor, simulation, or industry link that drew you in
Connect it to a concrete personal experience or goal
Show you understand what makes this course different from a general business degree elsewhere
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I looked closely at your second-year operations simulation where students actually run a mock supply chain against other teams, and that hands-on, competitive format is exactly how I learn best, rather than sitting through theory alone. I also read about the module on service operations, which speaks directly to a project I did analysing wait times at a community clinic near me. Most business courses treat operations as one module among many, but yours builds a whole specialism around it, which is what I actually want.

commonMistakes: Generic praise that would fit any university
Leaning on rankings or reputation alone
Confusing this course with a general management or logistics programme
followUps: What would you bring to a first-year operations project group?

question: Was there a specific moment that got you interested in how businesses actually run their operations?
lookingFor: An authentic, specific origin story rather than a vague or rehearsed claim of lifelong interest.

bullets: Describe one concrete moment or observation, not a lifelong vague interest
Explain what it revealed to you about how things function behind the scenes
Connect it to why you kept pursuing the interest afterward
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: During a school trip to a car assembly plant, I remember being far more interested in the conveyor timing and the way parts arrived exactly when needed than in the finished car itself. It struck me that the whole thing only worked because someone had designed the sequence down to the minute. I went home and started reading about how factories plan that kind of thing, and it turned into a genuine interest rather than a one-off school trip memory.

commonMistakes: Claiming a lifelong interest with no actual anecdote
Describing something generically business-related rather than operations-specific
Sounding rehearsed rather than genuinely curious
followUps: What did you do to explore that interest further afterward?

question: How would you explain the difference between operations management and general management to someone who has never heard the term?
lookingFor: A clear conceptual grasp of operations as the design and running of processes that turn inputs into outputs.

bullets: Define operations as the design and running of the processes that turn inputs into outputs
Note that it applies to services as much as manufacturing, not just factories
Distinguish it from other business functions like finance, marketing, or HR
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: General management covers the whole running of a business, from strategy to people to money, while operations management is specifically about how a business actually produces and delivers what it sells. It's not only about factories either, since a hospital scheduling surgeries or a bank processing loan applications is doing operations too. I think of it as the function responsible for turning resources into a reliable output, while marketing decides what to sell and finance decides how to pay for it.

commonMistakes: Conflating operations only with manufacturing or logistics
Giving a textbook definition with no real example
Failing to distinguish it from adjacent business functions
followUps: Can you give an example of operations in a service business rather than a factory?

question: Tell us about a project, internship, or part-time job where you saw operational decisions being made.
lookingFor: Real exposure with the ability to identify an actual operational trade-off, not just a job description.

bullets: Describe a specific role or observation, not a generic job summary
Identify a real operational trade-off you noticed, such as speed versus cost or quality versus throughput
Reflect honestly on what you would have done differently
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I did a two-week placement at a small print shop, and I noticed the owner constantly weighing whether to batch print jobs together to save setup time or run them individually to meet promised deadlines. Batching was cheaper per unit but meant some customers waited longer than they'd been told, which occasionally cost repeat business. If I'd been in charge, I would have tried separating jobs into a fast lane and a batch lane rather than treating every order the same way, so customers who needed speed could pay for it explicitly.

commonMistakes: Describing a job with no operational analysis at all
Exaggerating responsibility or scale of the experience
Offering no personal reflection or alternative view
followUps: What would you have changed if you were in charge?

question: Has any book, article, or case study shaped how you think about operations?
lookingFor: Evidence of genuine wider reading, with the ability to explain the idea accurately in your own words.

bullets: Name a specific source rather than a vague genre of reading
Summarise the core idea accurately and in your own words
Connect it to your own thinking or a real example
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I read Eliyahu Goldratt's 'The Goal', and the idea that stuck with me is that improving a process everywhere except its actual bottleneck doesn't increase overall output at all, it just creates more work sitting in a queue. It reframed how I look at any system, from a school cafeteria line to a factory floor, because my first instinct used to be to speed up whatever looked busiest rather than asking what's actually constraining the whole flow. I still think the book oversimplifies how hard it is to identify the real bottleneck in messier, real-world situations.

commonMistakes: Naming a book or article you can't actually explain
Choosing something unrelated to operations to sound impressive
Reciting a summary with no personal takeaway or critique
followUps: What's one thing you disagreed with or wanted to question in it?

question: Give us an example of a company you think is operationally excellent, and explain why.
lookingFor: Ability to identify concrete operational mechanisms, not just admiration for a well-known brand.

bullets: Name a specific company rather than a vague industry
Describe the actual operational mechanism, not just customer-facing strengths
Explain the trade-off the company manages well
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd pick Zara, because their whole model is built around a design-to-shelf cycle of a couple of weeks instead of the months most fashion retailers take. They deliberately keep some production close to their design centres in Spain rather than chasing the cheapest overseas labour everywhere, which costs more per unit but lets them react to what's actually selling and avoid the huge markdowns competitors face on unsold stock. It's a good example of a company choosing speed and responsiveness over pure cost minimisation, and having the operations to actually deliver on that choice.

commonMistakes: Vague brand praise with no operational detail
Describing marketing or product strength rather than operations
Naming a company you can't actually explain the mechanics of
followUps: What's a weakness or risk in their operating model?

question: Can you think of a time a company's operations failed publicly? What went wrong?
lookingFor: Analytical understanding of an operational root cause, not just recall of a news headline.

bullets: Give a specific, real example rather than a vague reference
Identify the actual operational root cause, not just the visible symptom
Suggest what could plausibly have prevented or reduced it
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I remember reading about a major airline's Christmas meltdown where a winter storm caused delays, but the real failure was that their crew scheduling system couldn't reassign staff fast enough, so thousands of flights kept cancelling for days after the weather had actually cleared. The storm was the trigger, but the operational cause was a scheduling process with almost no slack or backup capacity built in. A more resilient system would have kept some buffer crew and a manual override process ready for exactly this kind of disruption.

commonMistakes: Blaming the failure entirely on bad luck or external events
Failing to distinguish the operational cause from the trigger
Being too vague to show real understanding of what happened
followUps: How would you have designed a safeguard against that?

question: In simple terms, what is a supply chain?
lookingFor: A clear grasp of the full flow of goods, information, and money from raw material to end customer.

bullets: Describe it as the network of suppliers, producers, distributors, and retailers connecting raw material to customer
Mention that it involves flows of information and money, not just physical goods
Give a concrete example to illustrate it
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A supply chain is the whole network of organisations involved in turning raw materials into a product a customer can actually buy, from the supplier of raw cotton, to the factory that weaves and sews it, to the distributor, to the shop shelf. It's not just goods moving one direction either, since information about demand and orders flows back up the chain, and payments flow through it too. A coffee supply chain, for instance, runs all the way from a farm to a roaster to a cafe, with information about how much people are buying flowing back the other way.

commonMistakes: Reducing it to only 'getting products from factory to store'
Ignoring the information and money flows entirely
Giving no concrete example
followUps: What kinds of things can disrupt a supply chain?

question: What is a bottleneck in a process, and why does fixing the slowest step matter more than speeding up the others?
lookingFor: Correct understanding that overall throughput is limited by the slowest step, not the average speed of all steps.

bullets: Define a bottleneck as the step that limits the overall throughput of the whole process
Explain that speeding up a non-bottleneck step doesn't raise total output, it just creates idle capacity or a bigger queue elsewhere
Give a concrete example to show the logic
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A bottleneck is whichever step in a process is slowest relative to what's needed, and it sets the pace for everything downstream, no matter how fast the other steps run. If a cafe has one espresso machine but three people taking orders, speeding up the till doesn't get customers their coffee any faster, it just makes the queue at the machine longer. So the only way to actually increase how many customers get served is to fix the machine step itself, whether that's adding a second machine or changing how drinks are made.

commonMistakes: Assuming every slow step should be fixed equally
Missing the systemic throughput logic behind the concept
Giving a definition with no concrete example
followUps: How would you go about identifying the bottleneck in a process you can't directly observe?

question: Why might a company deliberately choose to hold less inventory, even though it risks running out of stock?
lookingFor: Understanding of the trade-off between holding costs and stockout risk, not an assumption that more stock is always safer.

bullets: Name the real costs of holding inventory, such as storage, tied-up capital, and the risk of obsolescence
Weigh that against the cost of a stockout, such as lost sales or a disappointed customer
Note that the right balance depends on how predictable demand is
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Holding extra stock isn't free, since it ties up cash that could be used elsewhere, needs warehouse space, and risks going unsold or out of date if demand shifts. So a company weighs that against the cost of occasionally running out, which might just mean a delayed order rather than a lost customer. For something like fashion where trends change fast, holding less stock and reordering often can actually be the safer choice, even though it raises the risk of a short-term stockout.

commonMistakes: Assuming more inventory is always the safer option
Ignoring the cost of capital tied up in stock
Treating the answer as universal rather than dependent on demand predictability
followUps: What is the economic order quantity idea trying to balance?

question: What do you understand by 'lean' in an operations context?
lookingFor: Correct understanding of lean as eliminating waste while preserving customer value, not simply cost-cutting.

bullets: Define lean as minimising waste in a process while preserving the value delivered to the customer
Mention its origin in the Toyota Production System
Give an example of a specific type of waste
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Lean is about identifying and removing anything in a process that doesn't add value for the customer, like unnecessary waiting, excess motion, or overproducing more than what's actually needed. It comes from the Toyota Production System, where they built the whole factory culture around continuously spotting and eliminating that kind of waste rather than just working harder. A common example is overproduction, where making more than customers currently want just creates inventory sitting around instead of actually helping anyone.

commonMistakes: Treating lean as simply cutting costs or headcount
Giving no example of an actual type of waste
Confusing lean with being cheap rather than efficient
followUps: Which type of waste do you think is most common in everyday student life?

question: How would you distinguish Lean from Six Sigma?
lookingFor: Understanding that Lean targets waste and flow while Six Sigma targets variation and defects, and that the two are often combined.

bullets: Explain that Lean focuses on removing waste and improving flow and speed
Explain that Six Sigma focuses on reducing variation and defects using statistical methods, often through a DMAIC cycle
Note that the two are frequently combined as Lean Six Sigma rather than treated as rivals
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Lean is mainly about speed and flow, stripping out steps that waste time or resources without adding value for the customer. Six Sigma is more about consistency, using data and statistics to find and reduce the causes of variation and defects, often following a structured cycle like define, measure, analyse, improve, control. They're not really competing approaches, since a lot of companies run them together as Lean Six Sigma, using Lean to speed a process up and Six Sigma to make sure it's also reliable.

commonMistakes: Treating Lean and Six Sigma as identical
Failing to mention variation or defects when describing Six Sigma
Being unable to give any example of where either applies
followUps: Which would you reach for first in a hospital emergency room, and why?

question: What is just-in-time production, and what is the main risk of relying on it?
lookingFor: Correct definition alongside awareness of the fragility trade-off, ideally with real-world relevance.

bullets: Define just-in-time as producing or receiving materials only as they're needed, rather than holding large stocks
Note the benefit is lower inventory and holding costs
Identify the main risk as fragility to any disruption in the supply chain
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Just-in-time means a company only brings in materials or produces parts right when they're needed for the next step, instead of stockpiling them in advance. It keeps inventory costs low and reduces waste from things sitting around unused. The downside became very visible during the pandemic and the chip shortage, where companies running very lean supply chains had almost no buffer, so a single delayed shipment could shut down an entire production line.

commonMistakes: Defining just-in-time with no mention of its downside
Confusing it with lean thinking generally rather than the specific inventory practice
Giving no real-world example of the risk
followUps: How did the pandemic change how companies think about just-in-time?

question: What's the difference between quality control and quality assurance?
lookingFor: A clear distinction between inspecting finished output and designing the process to prevent defects in the first place.

bullets: Define quality control as inspecting the finished product or output to catch defects, a reactive step
Define quality assurance as designing the process itself to prevent defects from happening, a proactive approach
Give an example of each
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Quality control is about checking the finished product or service after it's made, like a factory inspector pulling items off the line to test them. Quality assurance is more proactive, since it's about designing the whole process so defects are less likely to happen in the first place, like standardising how a machine is calibrated before a shift starts. A business that only relies on quality control ends up catching problems after they've already cost money to make, while quality assurance tries to stop that cost from happening at all.

commonMistakes: Treating the two terms as synonyms
Describing only one of the two concepts
Giving no concrete example of either
followUps: Which do you think matters more for a company just starting out, and why?

question: Why is demand forecasting such a central part of operations management, and what happens when it goes wrong?
lookingFor: Understanding that forecasts drive upstream capacity, inventory, and staffing decisions, and awareness that error is inevitable.

bullets: Link forecasting to the operational decisions it drives, such as capacity, inventory, and staffing
Name the consequence of getting it wrong in either direction, overproducing or underproducing
Acknowledge that no forecast is perfect, so operations has to manage uncertainty, not eliminate it
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Almost every operational decision, from how many staff to schedule to how much raw material to order, depends on some prediction of future demand, so a bad forecast doesn't just affect sales, it ripples through the whole operation. Underestimating demand means stockouts and lost sales, while overestimating means wasted inventory and idle capacity sitting around costing money. What I find interesting is that operations management isn't really about making forecasts perfect, since they never will be, it's about building processes flexible enough to absorb the error when the forecast is inevitably wrong.

commonMistakes: Treating forecasting as purely a marketing or sales concern
Not connecting forecasting to specific operational decisions
Assuming a perfect forecast is achievable
followUps: How might a company hedge against forecast error?

question: A small bakery makes 200 loaves a day but daily demand varies between 150 and 300. How would you think about planning their capacity?
lookingFor: Applied reasoning about the trade-off between lost sales and wasted capacity, without forcing a single confident answer.

bullets: Identify the core trade-off, lost sales on high-demand days versus wasted capacity or cost on low-demand days
Propose a few realistic options, such as flexible staffing, a small buffer stock, or pre-orders
Acknowledge that the right answer depends on the bakery's actual cost structure and what information isn't given
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: The real tension here is that building capacity for the busiest days means paying for equipment or staff that sit idle most of the time, while capping at the average means turning away customers on the good days. I'd want to know first whether the extra demand is predictable, like weekends being busier, because if so they could staff flexibly around a known pattern rather than building for the peak permanently. Another option would be taking pre-orders for busy days so some of that demand becomes plannable rather than a surprise, which reduces how much spare capacity they actually need to hold.

commonMistakes: Giving a single fixed answer with no discussion of the trade-off
Ignoring the cost of over-capacity entirely
Not asking what additional information would actually change the answer
followUps: What extra information would you want before deciding?

question: If you were asked to improve how a university library issues books, what's the first thing you'd actually do?
lookingFor: Instinct to observe and map the current process before proposing a solution, showing structured problem-solving.

bullets: Start by observing or mapping the current process end to end before suggesting any fix
Identify where the actual delay or friction occurs rather than assuming
Propose a testable, data-informed change rather than a guess
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Before suggesting anything, I'd want to actually watch the process happen a few times, from a student searching the catalogue to walking out with the book, because the real delay might be somewhere I wouldn't expect, like waiting for a librarian to manually log a return rather than the search itself. Once I could see where time was actually being lost, I'd look for the smallest realistic change that addresses that specific point, rather than jumping to something big like a whole new system. Then I'd want a way to measure whether the change actually helped, not just assume it did.

commonMistakes: Jumping straight to a solution like new technology without diagnosing the actual problem
Assuming the answer is more staff or more machines without evidence
Having no plan to measure whether the change worked
followUps: How would you know if your change actually worked?

question: An airport security line is getting longer even though the airport just added an extra scanner. What might be going on, and how would you investigate it?
lookingFor: Systems thinking that resists the obvious answer and reasons through where the true constraint might actually be.

bullets: Consider that the real bottleneck might not be the scanner at all, such as ID checks, staffing, or how passengers arrive in waves
Propose a way to gather data before jumping to a conclusion
Show awareness that adding capacity at the wrong point in a process doesn't fix the overall flow
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: My first instinct is that the scanner probably wasn't the actual constraint, so adding another one wouldn't help much, and the real slowdown might be happening at ID verification, staffing at peak times, or even just more flights being scheduled to land close together than before. I'd want to time each stage of the process separately, from ID check to tray loading to scanning to collecting bags, to see where passengers are actually queuing rather than assuming. It's a good reminder that adding capacity somewhere in a process only helps if you've actually confirmed that's where the constraint is.

commonMistakes: Assuming more scanners always solves a queue problem
Offering no way to actually test or gather evidence for the hypothesis
Treating the scenario as unsolvable rather than reasoning through it
followUps: What data would you want to collect first?

question: Is it always a good idea for a company to make its operations as efficient as possible? Can you think of a downside?
lookingFor: Mature understanding that hyper-efficient systems can become fragile, and ability to weigh trade-offs rather than give a one-sided answer.

bullets: Note that maximising efficiency usually means removing slack or buffer, which reduces resilience to disruption
Give a concrete example of an efficient system that broke under pressure
Argue for some deliberate balance rather than pure efficiency
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Efficiency almost always means cutting out slack, whether that's spare inventory, spare staff, or backup suppliers, because slack looks like waste on a spreadsheet. But that same slack is often what lets a business absorb a shock, and a lot of the supply chain failures during the pandemic happened to companies that had optimised so hard for cost that they had no buffer left when a single supplier went down. I don't think the answer is to abandon efficiency, but a company probably needs to decide deliberately where a bit of redundancy is worth paying for, rather than treating every bit of slack as pure waste.

commonMistakes: Treating efficiency as an unqualified good with no downside
Giving no concrete example of the risk
Failing to propose any alternative framing like resilience or redundancy
followUps: How would you decide how much slack is 'enough' for a given business?

question: What did events like the pandemic or the Suez Canal blockage teach you about how global operations work?
lookingFor: An applied, specific understanding of interdependence and risk in global supply chains, not a generic news summary.

bullets: Identify a specific mechanism, such as over-reliance on a single supplier, route, or region
Connect it to a concept like resilience, diversification, or buffer stock
Show it genuinely shaped their thinking rather than reciting a headline
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: What struck me about the Suez Canal blockage was how a single narrow physical route being blocked for less than a week could delay goods worth billions of dollars, which showed me how concentrated global shipping actually is around a few chokepoints. The pandemic taught a related lesson about relying heavily on one region for manufacturing, since a lockdown in one place rippled through industries that had nothing directly to do with it. It made me think differently about resilience, that spreading risk across multiple suppliers or routes can be worth the extra cost even if it looks less efficient on paper.

commonMistakes: Giving a vague answer like 'it showed supply chains are important'
Not naming a specific operational mechanism
Sounding like a recited news summary with no personal reflection
followUps: What's one change you'd expect companies to make permanently because of it?

question: How do you think automation and data are changing operations management as a field?
lookingFor: An informed, balanced view of technology's role, not sweeping claims that automation replaces the discipline entirely.

bullets: Give a concrete example, such as warehouse robotics, predictive maintenance, or real-time inventory tracking
Note it changes what operations managers actually do, shifting toward exception-handling and decisions, rather than eliminating the role
Show a balanced view rather than hype in either direction
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Warehouses using robotics to move stock and sensors that predict when a machine is about to fail before it actually breaks are good examples of how much routine tracking and reacting has already been automated. What I don't think changes is the need for judgement, because someone still has to decide what to do when the data shows something unusual, or when two automated systems give conflicting signals. I think the role shifts away from manually tracking things toward interpreting exceptions and making trade-off decisions, which is actually a more interesting version of the job, not a disappearing one.

commonMistakes: Making sweeping claims about automation with no concrete example
Assuming operations managers become obsolete
Ignoring the human judgement still required in the role
followUps: What's one operational task you think will still need a human in ten years?

question: A company can cut costs significantly by moving manufacturing to a supplier with weaker labour standards. How should an operations manager think about that decision?
lookingFor: Structured ethical reasoning weighing real commercial pressure against responsibility for the supply chain, not a snap verdict.

bullets: Acknowledge the genuine commercial pressure honestly, without pretending cost doesn't matter
Reason about the responsibility a company has for its extended supply chain, not just its own factory floor
Land on a practical position, such as audits or minimum standards, rather than an absolute yes or no
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I wouldn't pretend the cost pressure isn't real, because a company that ignores its costs entirely won't survive to help anyone. But I don't think a company gets to say conditions further down its own supply chain aren't its problem, especially once it knows about them, because it chose that supplier and benefits directly from the lower cost. My instinct is that the operations manager's job is to set minimum standards and actually audit for them before signing a contract, rather than either blindly chasing the cheapest option or refusing to outsource at all.

commonMistakes: Dismissing cost pressure as irrelevant or naive
Assuming not knowing the details is a valid excuse
Giving a snap absolute answer with no reasoning shown
followUps: Who do you think should be accountable if conditions turn out to be bad, the company or the supplier?

question: Tell us about a time you had to organise a process, event, or group task efficiently. What did you learn that you think applies to operations management?
lookingFor: Ability to extract a genuinely operations-relevant lesson from a real personal experience, not just a generic teamwork story.

bullets: Describe the real situation concretely, including the actual constraint like time, resources, or sequencing
Name the specific decision or trade-off you made
Connect it explicitly to an operations concept rather than leaving it generic
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I organised food and setup for a 200-person school fundraiser with a kitchen that could only realistically prep for eighty people at a time. Rather than trying to cook everything at once, I staggered the menu so half the dishes could be prepped a day ahead and only the ones that needed to be fresh were left for the morning, which was basically a scheduling and capacity problem in disguise. It taught me that most 'we don't have enough time or people' problems are actually sequencing problems, and thinking about what genuinely needs to happen last usually frees up more capacity than just working faster.

commonMistakes: Telling a generic teamwork story with no operational angle
Not naming a specific lesson connected to the field
Overstating the scale or importance of the achievement
followUps: What would you do differently next time?

question: If you had to redesign how your school cafeteria serves lunch to 500 students in a 40-minute break, what would you change?
lookingFor: Applied, creative operational thinking under a real constraint, with comfort reasoning aloud rather than freezing.

bullets: Identify the actual constraint, such as kitchen throughput, seating, or serving line speed, before proposing a fix
Propose a specific, testable change to address that constraint, such as staggered timing or separate lines by menu type
Acknowledge a trade-off or downside of your own proposed solution
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Before changing anything I'd want to know whether the actual constraint is how fast food can be served, or just that everyone tries to eat in the same twenty minutes in the middle of the break. If it's the second, I'd stagger lunch by year group across the full forty minutes rather than everyone arriving at once, which spreads demand without needing any extra kitchen capacity at all. The trade-off is that the group eating last gets a shorter effective break before their next class, so I'd want to rotate which group goes last across the week rather than fixing it permanently on one group.

commonMistakes: Proposing a solution before identifying the actual constraint
Ignoring the trade-offs or downsides of your own idea
Treating the scenario as unsolvable rather than reasoning through it
followUps: How would you measure whether your redesign actually worked?
